subject: A166913AB8014C26ABA2279F5D0A710F
introduction: “It is not our purpose to impose Bahá’í teachings upon others.” The guide follows a question often put to Bahá’ís: if their writings foresee a world order and even Bahá’í states, how is that to come about? The answers given by Shoghi Effendi and the Universal House of Justice are gradualness, the free decision of a population’s majority, the safeguarded rights of minorities, and obedience meanwhile to existing governments. The parables of the mustard seed, the leaven and the seed growing secretly are the Gospel’s pictures of such growth; the Qur’an’s “no compulsion in religion”, the Declaration’s “consent of the governed”, Jefferson’s statute and Locke’s letter are the tradition of consent the readings appeal to. “Compel them to come in”, Mill’s fear of the majority and Yeats’s rough beast are the grounds on which a reader might doubt, and Jesus’s “My kingdom is not of this world” puts the question to the whole expectation.
questions: What do the readings count as legitimate ways for a religion’s principles to become a society’s laws, and what as illegitimate?
Christianity became a state religion and then coerced. Which safeguards in the readings address that history, and are they enough?
Mill thought majorities as dangerous to liberty as kings. How does reading 13 respond?
Why does reading 19 warn beginners about the “promised glories”?

outside.why: Rulers and religious leaders to take counsel together. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord.
Grieve not over slow advance; consider the Cause of Christ, three centuries before its influence was seen. The least of all seeds becometh a tree.
The Kingdom founded in the invisible world becomes manifest by degrees. The kingdom of God cometh not with observation.
Gradually what is latent will appear. The seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
Political laws are not rigidly fixed. Confucius: if the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame.
The transformation will not come by imposing teachings. There is no compulsion in religion.
And to the Prophet himself, of those who would not believe: wouldst thou compel men until they are believers?
A state would adopt the Faith only through its people’s decision. Governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.
Bahá’ís will not allow their own institutions to supersede the government of their country. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers.

Not to persuade the powers that be to enact laws enforcing Bahá’í principles. The Virginia Statute: all men shall be free to profess, and by argument to maintain, their opinions in matters of religion.

“Compel them to come in”, a line in a parable, was Augustine’s warrant for the opposite policy, and Christendom’s for centuries. What in the readings would prevent the same development if Bahá’ís became a majority?
The rights of a non-Bahá’í minority in a Bahá’í state. Locke: neither Pagan nor Mahometan, nor Jew, ought to be excluded from the civil rights of the commonwealth because of his religion.
The Mosaic law on the resident alien is this reading’s remote ancestor. The stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you.

Bahá’ís will govern where they come to be the majority. Mill feared exactly the majority: over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign. Does consent by a majority answer his fear, or is reading 13 needed as well?

Non-partisan now; in the distant future, government. My kingdom is not of this world. Jesus refused a crown. How do the readings hold a religion without political ambition together with the expectation of a Bahá’í state?
A gradual process. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
The promised sovereignty is no worldly dominion; a warning to every beginner. Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.
The machinery of the Cause can incorporate whatever is later deemed necessary. Jefferson to Madison: the earth belongs in usufruct to the living.

Signs heralding the birth of the World Order. Yeats read the same signs with dread: what rough beast, its hour come round at last, slouches towards Bethlehem to be born? What makes the readings confident that what is being born is benign?
Only when the spirit has permeated the world will people enter in numbers. The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, till the whole was leavened.
The teachings are an instrument to be used. Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.

shortfall: Readings 5, 7, 10, 16, 18, 20, 23 and 25 restate the gradualness of the process or concern internal administration; nothing further was found for them.

ecclesiastes-end-better-than-beginning.text: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit
